claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys under harsh high-temperature exposure are governed by the ability to form stable, adherent multilayer oxide scales.
The formation of protective oxide scales is modulated by the balance between relative elemental redox potentials and atomic size mismatches.
An optimized balance of redox potentials and atomic size mismatches enhances protective scale formation compared with conventional alloys.
Systematically changing elemental ratios can adjust redox-potential differences and atomic-size mismatch in multiprincipal-element alloys.
Differences in elemental redox potentials direct preferential oxidation.
Atomic size mismatches influence diffusion kinetics.
The interplay between preferential oxidation and diffusion kinetics governs the nucleation and growth of stable, adherent oxide layers.
Stable, adherent oxide layers protect the underlying material.
Alloys having an optimized redox and atomic-size balance will develop more coherent and stable oxide scales than the conventional-alloy baseline.
More coherent and stable oxide scales will produce lower oxidation rates and improved material integrity relative to the conventional-alloy baseline.
Alloys with imbalanced redox and atomic-size parameters will exhibit nonuniform or premature oxide-scale failure.
The proposed behavior applies under cyclic high-temperature oxidation and controlled oxygen partial pressures typical of industrial high-temperature environments.
Microstructure and processing history may affect oxidation behavior.
